extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method, philosophers of science, and anyone learning the logic of induction and common fallacies
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and cautions for forming and assessing inductive generalizations and analogical inferences in scientific and moral inquiry, with examples of common fallacies (simple enumeration, false analogy, post hoc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish perceptions from inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: The universality of the confusion between perceptions and the inferences drawn from them; the power to discriminate one from the other is rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experienced cross-examiners know witnesses mix inference into narrative; ignorant observers habitually embed hypothesis in simple narratives. Training (e.g., painters, psychological analysts) is required to report sensations themselves rather than immediate inferences; failure to distinguish leads to misleading testimony and error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake inferences for direct intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid ascribing an intuitive character to judgments which are mere inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many deluded persons have believed they were directly inspired when they had merely drawn conclusions from sensations or internal feelings. A caution against treating inferences (even on great metaphysical questions) as if they were direct intuitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extrapolating local natural order to the universe at large
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferences from the order of nature existing on the earth or in the solar system to remote parts of the universe are groundless because phenomena elsewhere may follow different laws or none at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience on Earth cannot warrant universal claims about remote regions; be skeptical of universal generalizations beyond the domain of observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal negatives (claims of impossibility) lack empirical warrant except in special laws
rubrics_metrics.description: All propositions that assert impossibility (universal negatives) cannot be established by experience alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-existence observed so far only shows no adequate cause has manifested itself; only laws of number and extension (mathematical necessities) and the universal law of causality give sufficient warrant to assert impossibility within the same order of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not resolve radically different phenomena into one element without respect to qualitative distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The attempt to reduce qualitatively different phenomena (impressions differing in quality, not merely degree) to a single element or law is necessarily false if it ignores the inherent distinction perceived in consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It may be legitimate to show motions are conditions of heat or sensation; but even if physical antecedents are demonstrated, they do not explain the qualitative peculiarity (e.g., the sensation of color) — reduction can show causal conditions but not eliminate the distinctive nature of the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject simple enumeration (inductio per enumerationem simplicem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizing by simple enumeration — 'This, that, and the other A are B; I can think of no A which is not B; therefore every A is B' — is a puerile and precarious induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True induction must separate nature by rejections and exclusions and conclude affirmatively only after sufficient negatives; simple enumeration lacks elimination of alternatives and often rests on too few or readily available instances (examples: stereotyped 'common-sense' maxims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate empirical laws from causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not place empirical (mere customary succession) laws on the same footing of certainty as laws of cause and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical laws may describe regularities within observed limits and can admit refutation on empirical grounds; causal laws explain by reference to causes. Treat empirical generalizations as limited (often 'adjacent cases') unless underlying causes are established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware post hoc and cum hoc fallacies (causation from conjunction or sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer causation from mere chronological succession or mere conjunction (_post hoc, ergo propter hoc_ or _cum hoc, ergo propter hoc_).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: inferring that institutions caused national prosperity because prosperity occurred under them. Such conjunctions have little probative force without elimination of other antecedents or independent evidence that the supposed cause tends to produce the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid oversimple causal theories that ignore coexisting agents (false theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: False theory arises when conclusions are deduced from properties of a single supposed agent while overlooking other co-existing agents and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from medicine (attributing all disease to one principle like 'viscidity of the blood' or a single chemical cause) and politics (attributing social outcomes to one institutional feature). Such theories are prone to fatal errors when they oversimplify multifactorial phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat analogical arguments as at best inconclusive presumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument from analogy (inferring B in a case because it holds in a somewhat similar case) provides only a limited increase in probability unless a causal or law-like connection between the shared property and the inferred property is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: inferring that other planets are inhabited because the Earth is; analogy increases probability only slightly unless one can assign or show A is a condition or cause of B. If a causal link is shown, the inference becomes an induction from a law rather than mere analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two distinct fallacies of analogy: overrating and illicit transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: False analogies occur either by overrating the probative force of a (possibly correct) analogical argument, or by inferring resemblance in one respect from resemblance in another when evidence tends to disconnect them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overrating is common among minds that perceive few analogies and thus overweight them; illicit transfer is exemplified by trying to derive political conclusions from family analogies (paternal government → despotism) where the crucial supporting properties (affection, wisdom) are absent in the political case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogical reasoning must consider whether the resemblance concerns the relevant properties (avoid irrelevant resemblances)
rubrics_metrics.description: When using analogy, ensure the shared properties are materially connected to the inferred property; irrelevant or superficial resemblances do not justify the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comparing precious metals to corn/coal ignores that the 'utility' of metals for coin depends on scarcity (value), a materially relevant property, whereas abundance would not change the utility of corn the same way — the analogy fails on the essential point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit empirical generalizations to adjacent cases and specify causal conditions for prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical generalizations (e.g., about human society) are often valid only within certain spatial, temporal, or circumstantial bounds ('adjacent cases'); to predict beyond these, one must ascertain the actual causes producing the observed changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims like 'the species is necessarily progressive' are empirical summaries, not causal laws. To make reliable future predictions, identify and analyze the determinate causes that produced past changes and those that may check or counteract them.
